cards.term: What was the Second Great Awakening?
cards.def: It was the evangelical revival, already underway on the frontier, whose more optimistic view of human potential—that all men and women might choose and win salvation—fostered mass conversions and ambitious programs for reforming individuals and society.

cards.term: How did evangelical doctrine change after about 1800?
cards.def: Before about 1800 most American evangelicals embraced Calvinism, the belief that God had already determined who was damned or saved, but heirs of a revolution that celebrated equality, free will, and reason moved toward the more democratic belief that each individual should take an active responsibility for redemption.

cards.term: Who was Charles Grandison Finney, and what were the "new measures"?
cards.def: Finney was the founder of modern revivalism, and he systematically used techniques developed in frontier camp meetings: protracted meetings night after night, praying for sinners by name, encouraging women to testify in public, and placing those struggling with conversion on the anxious bench.

cards.term: What social issues attracted the attention of reformers?
cards.def: Reformers attacked drinking, worked for Sunday schools, missions, and Sabbath observance, created asylums for the mentally ill, expanded public schooling, formed utopian communities, and, most radically, demanded the immediate end of slavery and new rights for women.

cards.term: What was the temperance movement, and why did it spread?
cards.def: It was the campaign to curb or prohibit alcohol at a time when consumption had reached more than five gallons of distilled liquor a year, because democracy seemed to need sober voters, factories needed sober workers, and the cause appealed to women as a way to defend the home.

cards.term: Why were Lyman Beecher and his family a significant force in American religion and reform?
cards.def: Beecher was a celebrated conservative evangelical who sought to restore the moral government of God through revivals and the Benevolent Empire, while his children, including Harriet Beecher Stowe, pushed on to attack slavery, the family, and women's legal subordination.

cards.term: How had the role of women in the public and private sphere changed?
cards.def: The cult of domesticity confined middle-class wives to a private sphere as moral "angels" of the household, yet women dominated revivals by about three to two and used church and benevolent societies to gain public experience holding office, raising money, and organizing reform.

cards.term: How would you summarize the early women's rights movement?
cards.def: After Stanton and Mott were forced to sit behind a curtain at a London antislavery convention, they organized the 1848 Seneca Falls conference, whose Declaration of Sentiments declared that "all men and women are created equal" and called for education, property rights, legal equality, and, most controversially, the vote.

cards.term: How had religion become increasingly polarized between Protestants and Catholics?
cards.def: Evangelicals stressed inward conversion and individual Bible reading and looked toward an imminent millennium, while Catholics emphasized outward observances, church teaching, and the sacraments; anti-Catholic tracts such as the Maria Monk book and riots in Charlestown and Philadelphia followed the growth of Catholicism.

cards.term: What was the American Renaissance, and who were some of its major figures?
cards.def: It was the coming of age of a distinctive American literature after Emerson's call in "The American Scholar," and its major figures included Emerson, Thoreau, Whitman, Hawthorne, and Melville, who explored nature, the individual, and the costs of civilization.

cards.term: How did Unitarianism and Transcendentalism compare?
cards.def: Unitarians were rational Christians who denied Jesus's divinity, disliked revival emotionalism, and still shared evangelicals' faith in human agency and social betterment, while Transcendentalists, many of them former Unitarians, went further by elevating feeling over reason and teaching that every person contained a spark of divinity.

cards.term: Who were the major communitarian reformers, and what were some utopian communities?
cards.def: Secular examples included George Ripley's Brook Farm, Robert Owen's New Harmony, and Fourierist settlements, while religious ones included the celibate Shakers led from Ann Lee's tradition and John Humphrey Noyes's Oneida Community, which practiced complex marriage.

cards.term: What did abolitionists want?
cards.def: They wanted an immediate end to slavery as a sin, rejected gradual emancipation and colonization, refused compensation for slaveholders, and, in Garrison's program, sought to convince Southerners by moral suasion while also championing rights for African Americans.

cards.term: What role did women and Blacks play in the abolitionist movement?
cards.def: Free African Americans were always an important source of support—they were a majority of The Liberator's subscribers and led much of the Underground Railroad—while women, drawn from church work, became so central that Garrison's endorsement of their right to hold office helped split the movement, and some went on to launch women's rights.

cards.term: Why did abolitionism remain controversial even in the North?
cards.def: It attacked powerful interests, championed African Americans in the face of pervasive racism, and provoked mobs, including the seizure of Garrison in Boston and the murder of Elijah Lovejoy, so abolitionists always remained a small minority of northern society.

cards.term: Why did the abolitionist movement split in 1840?
cards.def: More-conservative reformers wanted to work through churches and politics, but Garrison embraced perfectionism, denounced the Constitution as "a covenant with death and an agreement with hell," and packed a convention to support women holding office, after which Lewis Tappan's group formed the American and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society.

cards.term: What was the Maine Law, and how did temperance affect the parties?
cards.def: It was the 1851 statewide prohibition law that authorized search and seizure and stiff penalties for selling liquor, and because Whigs and Democrats both included wets and dries, the issue increased party switching and helped dissolve old party loyalties.

cards.term: What was the gag rule, and why did it backfire?
cards.def: In 1836 the House automatically tabled any petition dealing with slavery, but that tactical blunder let abolitionists defend white civil liberties as well as attack slavery, broadening their appeal until the rule was repealed in 1844.

cards.term: How did reform shake the party system?
cards.def: Temperance, abolition, and women's rights increasingly sought legislation, the Liberty Party ran James Birney in 1840, and moral questions made it harder for the two national parties to hold supporters in both sections, weakening the Jacksonian party system.

cards.term: Why did the reform impulse find little support in the South?
cards.def: Despite the strength of evangelicalism there, reform movements were discredited by their association with abolitionism, and the South increasingly appeared to be a unique society with its own distinctive way of life.

cards.term: What did Finney mean by saying a revival "is not a miracle"?
cards.def: Unlike earlier revivalists who treated revivals as god-sent outpourings of grace, Finney viewed them as the result of human agency, "a purely scientific result of the right use of constituted means," and told the anxious, "Do it!"

cards.term: What was Uncle Tom's Cabin, and who wrote it?
cards.def: It was the most successful piece of antislavery literature in the nation's history, written in the 1850s by Harriet Beecher Stowe, a daughter of Lyman Beecher who, unlike her father, treated slavery as an unjust social institution that had to be abolished.
